items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we toss a ball vertically upwards with initial velocity [MATH: u=24.5\,\textrm{m/s},] as shown below. How do we determine the ball's height after [MATH: 1] second?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6b9afc976e1b4aaeabc27c68d9598c6f]

Content:
The displacement of an object after being projected vertically upward can be modeled using the equation
[MATH: s=ut + \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2.]

Content:
Let's recall what each variable represents:

Content:
- [MATH: s] is the displacement from the starting position, measured in meters.
- [MATH: u] is the initial velocity, measured in meters per second.
- [MATH: t] is time, measured in seconds.
- [MATH: g=-9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2] is the acceleration due to gravity.

Content:
Important: In this situation, we take the constant [MATH: g] to be negative because the ball moves against gravity. In other words, the ball travels upward, yet gravity is trying to pull the ball back down to Earth.

Content:
To determine the height of the ball after one second, we substitute [MATH: u = 24.5, t=1,] and [MATH: g=-9.8] into our equation for [MATH: s,] and evaluate:

Content:
[MATH: s|= ut + (1)/(2)gt^{2}; = (24.5)(1) + (1)/(2)(− 9.8)(1)^{2}; = 24.5 − 4.9; = 19.6]

Content:
Therefore, after one second, the ball is [MATH: 19.6\,\textrm{m}] above the ground.

items.title: Upwards Vertical Motion: Solving for Displacement

sections.normalized_html: A cannonball is shot straight up from a platform [MATH: 5 \, \textrm{m}] above the ground with an initial velocity of [MATH: 22 \, \textrm{m/s}.] How high above the ground is the cannonball after [MATH: 3] seconds?
sections.readable_text: A cannonball is shot straight up from a platform [MATH: 5 \, \textrm{m}] above the ground with an initial velocity of [MATH: 22 \, \textrm{m/s}.] How high above the ground is the cannonball after [MATH: 3] seconds?

sections.normalized_html:
To solve this problem, we use the formula [MATH: s=ut+\dfrac{1}{2}gt^2,] where [MATH: s] is the displacement, measured from the starting position in the direction of the initial motion, [MATH: u] is the initial velocity, [MATH: t] is the time since the beginning of the motion, and [MATH: g] is the acceleration due to gravity.

Let's summarize the information we have:

  • The initial velocity of the cannonball is [MATH: u=22\,\textrm{m/s}.]

  • The cannonball is moving for [MATH: t=3\,\textrm{s}.]

  • The acceleration due to gravity is [MATH: g=-9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2.] Notice that [MATH: g] is negative since the cannonball's motion acts against gravity.

Substituting these values into the formula, we obtain the following: [MATH: s|= (22) ⋅ 3 − (1)/(2)(9.8) ⋅ (3)^{2}; = 66 − 4.9(9); = 66 − 44.1; = 21.9]

Therefore, after [MATH: 3] seconds the cannonball is [MATH: 21.9\,\textrm{m}] above the platform.

Finally, we add the height of the [MATH: 5\,\textrm{m}] platform: [MATH: 5 + 21.9 = 26.9 \,\textrm{m}]

Therefore, after [MATH: 3] seconds, the cannonball is [MATH: 26.9\,\textrm{m}] above the ground.

sections.normalized_html: An object is projected vertically upwards, attaining a height of [MATH: 40 \, \textrm{m}] in [MATH: 2\,\textrm{s}.] What was the initial velocity of the object?

sections.normalized_html:
To solve this problem, we use the formula [MATH: s=ut+\dfrac{1}{2}gt^2,] where [MATH: s] is the displacement, measured from the starting position in the direction of the initial motion, [MATH: u] is the initial velocity, [MATH: t] is the time since the beginning of the motion, and [MATH: g] is the acceleration due to gravity.

Let's summarize the information we have:

  • The object is moving for [MATH: t=2\,\textrm{s}.]

  • The displacement of the object is [MATH: s=40\, \textrm{m}.]

  • The acceleration due to gravity is [MATH: g=-9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2.] Notice that [MATH: g] is negative since the object's motion acts against gravity.

Substituting these values into the formula and solving for [MATH: u,] we obtain the following:

[MATH: s|= ut + (1)/(2)gt^{2}; (40)|= u(2) + (1)/(2)(− 9.8)(2)^{2}; 40|= 2u − 19.6; 59.6|= 2u; 29.8|= u; u|= 29.8]

Therefore, the initial velocity of the object was [MATH: 29.8\,\textrm{m/s}.]

items.title: Calculating the Maximum Height of an Object

key_prerequisites.name: The Axis of Symmetry of a Parabola

sections.normalized_html: A marble is projected vertically upward with an initial velocity of [MATH: 15.7 \, \textrm{m/s}.] Find the maximum height reached by the marble. Round your answer to one decimal place.
sections.readable_text: A marble is projected vertically upward with an initial velocity of [MATH: 15.7 \, \textrm{m/s}.] Find the maximum height reached by the marble. Round your answer to one decimal place.

sections.normalized_html:
To solve this problem, we use the formula [MATH: s=ut+\dfrac{1}{2}gt^2,] where [MATH: s] is the displacement, measured from the starting position in the direction of the initial motion, [MATH: u] is the initial velocity, [MATH: t] is the time since the beginning of the motion, and [MATH: g] is the acceleration due to gravity.

Let's summarize the information we have:

  • The initial velocity of the marble is [MATH: u=15.7\,\textrm{m/s}.]

  • The acceleration due to gravity is [MATH: g=-9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2.] Notice that [MATH: g] is negative since the marble's motion acts against gravity.

Substituting these values into the formula, we obtain the following:

[MATH: s|= ut + (1)/(2)gt^{2}; = 15.7t + (1)/(2)(− 9.8)t^{2}; = 15.7t − 4.9t^{2}; = − 4.9t^{2} + 15.7t]

The function [MATH: s(t)] is a downward parabola, and the maximum height corresponds to the vertex of the parabola.

The [MATH: t]-coordinate of the vertex can be found using the formula [MATH: t= -\dfrac{b}{2a}.]

In our case, we have [MATH: a = -4.9] and [MATH: b=15.7], which gives

[MATH: t=-\dfrac{15.7}{2(-4.9)}=1.602\,040... \approx 1.6020.]

So the marble attains its maximum height at [MATH: t=1.6020] seconds. The height of the marble at this time is

[MATH: s|= − 4.9t^{2} + 15.7t; = − 4.9(1.6020)^{2} + 15.7(1.6020); = 12.576...; ≈ 12.6m.]

Therefore, the marble reached a maximum height of [MATH: 12.6\,\textrm{m}] in [MATH: 1.6\,\textrm{s}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we toss a ball vertically upwards with initial velocity [MATH: u=24.5\,\textrm{m/s},] as shown below. How do we determine the ball's height after [MATH: 1] second?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6b9afc976e1b4aaeabc27c68d9598c6f]

Content:
The displacement of an object after being projected vertically upward can be modeled using the equation
[MATH: s=ut + \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2.]

Content:
Let's recall what each variable represents:

Content:
- [MATH: s] is the displacement from the starting position, measured in meters.
- [MATH: u] is the initial velocity, measured in meters per second.
- [MATH: t] is time, measured in seconds.
- [MATH: g=-9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2] is the acceleration due to gravity.

Content:
Important: In this situation, we take the constant [MATH: g] to be negative because the ball moves against gravity. In other words, the ball travels upward, yet gravity is trying to pull the ball back down to Earth.

Content:
To determine the height of the ball after one second, we substitute [MATH: u = 24.5, t=1,] and [MATH: g=-9.8] into our equation for [MATH: s,] and evaluate:

Content:
[MATH: s|= ut + (1)/(2)gt^{2}; = (24.5)(1) + (1)/(2)(− 9.8)(1)^{2}; = 24.5 − 4.9; = 19.6]

Content:
Therefore, after one second, the ball is [MATH: 19.6\,\textrm{m}] above the ground.

---

Item 2 — Example: Upwards Vertical Motion: Solving for Displacement

Example Prompt:
A cannonball is shot straight up from a platform [MATH: 5 \, \textrm{m}] above the ground with an initial velocity of [MATH: 22 \, \textrm{m/s}.] How high above the ground is the cannonball after [MATH: 3] seconds?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To solve this problem, we use the formula
[MATH: s=ut+\dfrac{1}{2}gt^2,]
where [MATH: s] is the displacement, measured from the starting position in the direction of the initial motion, [MATH: u] is the initial velocity, [MATH: t] is the time since the beginning of the motion, and [MATH: g] is the acceleration due to gravity.

Let's summarize the information we have:

- The initial velocity of the cannonball is [MATH: u=22\,\textrm{m/s}.]
- The cannonball is moving for [MATH: t=3\,\textrm{s}.]
- The acceleration due to gravity is [MATH: g=-9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2.] Notice that [MATH: g] is negative since the cannonball's motion acts against gravity.

Substituting these values into the formula, we obtain the following:
[MATH: s|= (22) ⋅ 3 − (1)/(2)(9.8) ⋅ (3)^{2}; = 66 − 4.9(9); = 66 − 44.1; = 21.9]

Therefore, after [MATH: 3] seconds the cannonball is [MATH: 21.9\,\textrm{m}] above the platform.

Finally, we add the height of the [MATH: 5\,\textrm{m}] platform:
[MATH: 5 + 21.9 = 26.9 \,\textrm{m}]

Therefore, after [MATH: 3] seconds, the cannonball is [MATH: 26.9\,\textrm{m}] above the ground.

where [MATH: s] is the displacement, measured from the starting position in the direction of the initial motion, [MATH: u] is the initial velocity, [MATH: t] is the time since the beginning of the motion, and [MATH: g] is the acceleration due to gravity.

- The object is moving for [MATH: t=2\,\textrm{s}.]
- The displacement of the object is [MATH: s=40\, \textrm{m}.]
- The acceleration due to gravity is [MATH: g=-9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2.] Notice that [MATH: g] is negative since the object's motion acts against gravity.

Substituting these values into the formula and solving for [MATH: u,] we obtain the following:

[MATH: s|= ut + (1)/(2)gt^{2}; (40)|= u(2) + (1)/(2)(− 9.8)(2)^{2}; 40|= 2u − 19.6; 59.6|= 2u; 29.8|= u; u|= 29.8]

Item 10 — Example: Calculating the Maximum Height of an Object

Example Prompt:
A marble is projected vertically upward with an initial velocity of [MATH: 15.7 \, \textrm{m/s}.] Find the maximum height reached by the marble. Round your answer to one decimal place.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To solve this problem, we use the formula
[MATH: s=ut+\dfrac{1}{2}gt^2,]
where [MATH: s] is the displacement, measured from the starting position in the direction of the initial motion, [MATH: u] is the initial velocity, [MATH: t] is the time since the beginning of the motion, and [MATH: g] is the acceleration due to gravity.

Let's summarize the information we have:

- The initial velocity of the marble is [MATH: u=15.7\,\textrm{m/s}.]
- The acceleration due to gravity is [MATH: g=-9.8\,\textrm{m/s}^2.] Notice that [MATH: g] is negative since the marble's motion acts against gravity.

Substituting these values into the formula, we obtain the following:

[MATH: s|= ut + (1)/(2)gt^{2}; = 15.7t + (1)/(2)(− 9.8)t^{2}; = 15.7t − 4.9t^{2}; = − 4.9t^{2} + 15.7t]

The function [MATH: s(t)] is a downward parabola, and the maximum height corresponds to the vertex of the parabola.

[IMG: /graphics/c2d364654030b19d65cb43daf5afe988]

The [MATH: t]-coordinate of the vertex can be found using the formula
[MATH: t= -\dfrac{b}{2a}.]

In our case, we have [MATH: a = -4.9] and [MATH: b=15.7], which gives

[MATH: t=-\dfrac{15.7}{2(-4.9)}=1.602\,040... \approx 1.6020.]

So the marble attains its maximum height at [MATH: t=1.6020] seconds. The height of the marble at this time is

[MATH: s|= − 4.9t^{2} + 15.7t; = − 4.9(1.6020)^{2} + 15.7(1.6020); = 12.576...; ≈ 12.6m.]

Therefore, the marble reached a maximum height of [MATH: 12.6\,\textrm{m}] in [MATH: 1.6\,\textrm{s}.]
